credits.bin.title: BÍN: Database of Icelandic Morphology
credits.bin.text: Every inflected form in TÖLVA comes from the DMII Core (BÍN-kjarninn) of the Árni Magnússon Institute for Icelandic Studies, bin.arnastofnun.is. License: CC BY-SA 4.0. Paradigms are shown exactly as published, without changes. The 23 indeclinable numerals that the DMII Core lacks were confirmed in the full BÍN through Ylhýra.
credits.wikt.text: Glosses, IPA, etymology and Norwegian translations come from Wiktionary by its contributors, extracted by kaikki.org (wiktextract). License: CC BY-SA 4.0. For the few course words Wiktionary gives no Norwegian for, and where its Norwegian gloss is wrong (another sense or word class, or a misspelling), the Bokmål gloss was written for TÖLVA; every word of every Bokmål gloss is a form in Bokmålsordboka. The etymologies were translated into Bokmål by hand for TÖLVA, under the same license, and are shown when the app is in Norwegian.
credits.tatoeba.text: Example sentences and translations come from Tatoeba. License: CC BY 2.0 FR. Each sentence in the app links to its page and names its author. Every sentence was checked with GreynirCorrect before use. Tatoeba has a Norwegian Bokmål translation for only a few of these sentences; for the others, the Bokmål translation was written by hand for TÖLVA, from the Icelandic with Tatoeba's English translation as a check, and every word in it is a form in Bokmålsordboka. For topics Tatoeba has few sentences on, a few sentences were made for TÖLVA from a Tatoeba sentence by replacing one word, and checked with GreynirCorrect like the others: they name the original's author, link to the original and say that a word was changed, and their English translation was written for TÖLVA from the original's.
credits.audio.title: Recordings
credits.audio.text: Word recordings are played from Wikimedia Commons, most of them made with Lingua Libre. Each recording shows its speaker and license where it is played.
credits.tts.title: Generated voice
credits.tts.text: Words and sentences without a human recording are spoken by the generated voice the learner chooses (Steinn, Salka, Búi or Ugla), made ahead of time with Piper (GPL-3.0; a build tool, not part of the website). The Icelandic Piper voices were trained on the Talrómur corpus by Reykjavík University (CC BY 4.0). The generated audio is offered under CC BY 4.0 with that credit; sentence audio speaks Tatoeba sentences, credited above. Compare all four voices.
credits.music.title: Music
credits.music.text: The menu music is composed and synthesized in your browser by TÖLVA's own code (MIT license): no recordings, samples or existing melodies. Its rules for harmony and melody follow Open Music Theory (Gotham and others), and its tvísöngur sections follow descriptions of Icelandic two-part singing, listed in the Music lab.
credits.bm.text: The Norwegian bridge links course words to their Bokmål relatives and the Old Norse words behind them: Bokmålsordboka, Universitetet i Bergen og Språkrådet, ordbøkene.no, CC BY 4.0. Only the Bokmål lemma, the article number and the Old Norse word are stored.

music.iceland.title: Icelandic in the music
music.iceland.tvisongur: Every song has a tvísöngur section. Tvísöngur is Iceland's own two-part singing: two voices sing note against note in parallel fifths, slowly, cross and meet on the same note, and the second voice usually ends on the note the first began with; the last note is held (Björg Blondal, 2022; International Research Center for Traditional Polyphony). Here two synthesized voices sing it.
music.iceland.modes: The modes come from Icelandic folk song. Of the songs Bjarni Þorsteinsson collected in Íslenzk þjóðlög (1906 to 1909), around 250 are in the Lydian mode (Bjarki Sveinbjörnsson, 2009), and tvísöngur songs are most often in F Lydian or D Dorian, the oldest mostly in D Dorian (Blondal). Dreamwave is in F Lydian, and the Happy mood sings its tvísöngur in D Dorian. Cyberpunk is in the Phrygian mode, the mode of Krummi svaf í klettagjá (Wikipedia).
music.iceland.langspil: Dreamwave begins on a langspil, the Icelandic drone zither: one melody string over drone strings, here sounding the keynote and its fifth (Wikipedia).
music.how.title: How the songs are built
music.how.form: Each song has an intro, verses, choruses and the tvísöngur, in sections of eight bars. The chord loops are well-known patterns of pop music, such as Am, F, C, G in Synthwave and the heroic A♭, B♭, C that ends the Happy chorus (Open Music Theory).
music.how.melody: Verse melodies are periods: four bars that end open, answered by four bars that start the same way and end on the keynote. Chorus melodies are sentences: a short idea, its repeat, and a busier ending. Notes on the beat belong to the chord, notes between beats move by step, each phrase has one high point, and the last note is approached by step. Each day brings new melodies, and every one is checked against these rules.
music.how.sound: Every sound is synthesized as you listen: drum machine, bass, pads, arpeggio, lead and the two voices. When a song ends, a new one is composed.
